hints: Notice all four options are around $10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and compare them with the elementary charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Recall that charge is quantised, so any isolated charge must equal $Q = ne$ where $n$ is a positive or negative integer.
Divide each value such as $-2.4 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and check which division does not give a whole number.
walkthrough: Identify the rule: charge on a single carrier is quantised in multiples of the elementary charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Write the test as $n = Q/e$, where $n$ must be an integer such as $\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3$.
For $-2.4 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n = -2.4/1.6 = -1.5$, which is not an integer and violates $Q = ne$.
Therefore $-2.4 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ cannot be the charge on a charge carrier. This is option C.

A.explanation: This is $-3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, an integer multiple of the elementary charge, so it can exist.

B.explanation: This is $-2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, an integer multiple of the elementary charge, so it can exist.

C.explanation: This is $-1.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, not an integer multiple of the elementary charge, so it cannot exist.

D.explanation: This is $+2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, an integer multiple of the elementary charge, so it can exist.
